newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: No comment from Air NZ on profit down-grade story.
newsitem.headline: No comment from Air NZ on profit down-grade story.

text.p: Air New Zealand Ltd on Wednesday declined to comment on a newspaper article suggesting high fuel costs and the strong New Zealand dollar would prompt analysts to lower their forecasts for the carrier's June 1997 year profit.
The New Zealand Herald said latest indications suggested the carrier's earnings would be around NZ$180 million, assuming that jet fuel prices fall and the dollar softens.
But it quoted analysts saying that any expectations of the dollar easing had been deferred following last week's disappointing inflation data.
The price of Air New Zealand's A shares fell three cents to $2.76 on Wednesday after the article was published. The B shares, able to be owned by non-New Zealanders, fell four cents to $3.92.

Merrill Lynch broker Ian Waddell said the share price softness could also be due to Air NZ's half owned Australian associate Ansett failing to win as many beyond rights concessions in Japan as had been hoped for.
Expectations for Air New Zealand's profit this year started at around $200 million after a 13 percent slump in June 1996 year earnings to $225 million was announced last September.
In December, that figure was lowered to a market average of $190 million.

Analysts said that an apparent lack of progress on Air New Zealand's cost-cutting exercise was adding to its woes. In September the company indicated it was seeking cost reductions totalling $100 million over the year.
The strong Kiwi dollar had a significant impact on Air New Zealand's earnings, brokers told the Herald. Some $1.6 billion of Air New Zealand's annual revenue of $3 billion came from overseas.
Since July, the New Zealand dollar had risen by around 10 percent against the Japanese yen.

Arthur Lim of Ord Minnett told the Herald he expected some softness in Air New Zealand's share price because of the new round of profit down-grades. "But the question is, will earnings bounce the following year?"
Air New Zealand said it could not comment on the report because it was too close to its half-year profit announcement due in mid-February.
